newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin sees more state ties with Orthodox Church.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sees more state ties with Orthodox Church.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin pledged on Sunday to promote freedom of conscience in post-communist Russia and said he was sure that state cooperation with the Orthodox Church would grow.

In two separate messages issued at the start of Orthodox Easter, Yeltsin praised the church's contribution to Russian society and told its followers that Russians of all faiths should work together to rebuild the country.

"The Russian Orthodox Church occupies a special place in the life of Russian society, in developing and strengthening its spiritual and moral values and in achieving civil peace and accord," he said in a message to Moscow Patriarch Alexiy.

"I am sure that fruitful cooperation between Russian state structures and the Orthodox Church will be further extended and strengthened," he said, thanking the church for its charity work and contribution to the development of Russian culture.

The Orthodox Church, hounded by Russia's former communist rulers, has undergone a vigorous revival since the old system collapsed in 1991 and people packed churches on Saturday night for the most important ceremonies of its year.
At the Bogoyavlenski Sobor (Epiphany Cathedral) in Moscow, crowds queued for hours to attend the overnight service, conducted by Patriarch Alexiy and attended by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Yeltsin, who normally goes to the church at Easter, was on holiday in the Black Sea resort of Sochi.
Police patrols were stepped up around the cathedral and officers with sniffer dogs searched the building, elaborately decorated with icons, for explosives.
In a technological breakthough for the church, the service was being transmitted live over the Internet global computer network.
The Orthodox Church, an integral part of state before the 1917 Bolshevik revolution, is seeking to strengthen its role in Russia.
Church leaders say they do not want a fusion of church and state and they describe relations with members of other established faiths, including Moslems, Jews, Buddhists and Catholics, as good.

But some representatives of other beliefs are worried by what they say are sporadic cases of discrimination at a local level in favour of the Orthodox Church, whose strong historical and cultural roots have caught the imagination of Russian nationalists.
In his message to Orthodox Christians, Yeltsin appeared to be addressing those fears when he said that cooperation between faiths was essential for civil and ethnic peace.

"I believe that all Russians, regardless of their religious convictions, will work together to ensure that this year...becomes an important landmark on the path of spiritual and moral renewal of our Fatherland," he said.
"I intend to further aid successful cooperation between the state and religious organisations, the consistent realisation of the freedom of conscience and faith as laid down in the constitution."
